result.summary: Roman envoys led by Metellus and later Appius meddle in the quarrel between the Spartans and the Achæan League, and each time the Achæans are treated unfairly. The Romans restore Spartan exiles, rebuild Sparta's walls follow, and order the return of Messenian and Achæan exiles, which the Achæans resentfully accept.

scenes.title: Metellus and the Achæan Rebuff
scenes.summary: Metellus asks the Achæans to treat Sparta kindly, but they demand a Senate decree. Metellus reports unfavorably in Rome, where Areus and Alcibiades add accusations and the Achæans condemn them to death.
scenes.stakes: The Achæans risk Roman displeasure by refusing to yield without a Senate decree.

scenes.title: Appius Judges for Sparta
scenes.summary: Appius arrives with Areus and Alcibiades; Lycortas defends the Achæans but is jeered. Rome sends Appius again and restores Spartan exiles, leaving Sparta in the League, and Sparta rebuilds its walls.
scenes.stakes: The Achæans stand to lose their authority over Sparta and their treaty rights.

scenes.title: Exiles Return by Roman Order
scenes.summary: The restored Spartans persuade Messenian and Achæan exiles to appeal to Rome. Appius favours them, and the Senate orders their restoration, which the Achæans bitterly accept.
scenes.stakes: The Achæans suffer injustice and the loss of their credit for past service to Rome.

notable_quotes.reason: Sums up Achæan bitterness at Roman ingratitude after their loyal service.

analysis.text: Rome's growing control over Greece appears through its partial arbitration, which favours Sparta and erodes Achæan autonomy.
The episode belongs to the 180s–170s BC, when Rome used Greek quarrels to weaken the Achæan League, a prelude to its later destruction.

language_notes.text: "Except they were armed with" means unless they came bearing a Senate decree; the Achæans refuse any discussion without formal Roman authorization.
"Hauteur" means haughty arrogance; Metellus took the Achæan reply as disrespect toward Rome.
"Inveighed" means spoke against violently, attacking with bitter words.
"Plenipotentiaries" are envoys with full power to decide the matter on behalf of their government.
"Absconded before judgment" means they fled before trial and were condemned in their absence; Rome cancelled those penalties.
Capital cases were to be tried by foreign courts, i.e. outside Sparta and the League; other cases could be handled locally or by the League.
"Unkindest cut of all" is an idiom for the most hurtful blow, here Rome's favouring of exiles.

context_notes.text: Nabis was the tyrant of Sparta, defeated by Rome and the Achæans; he was killed around 192 BC. Areus and Alcibiades were Spartan exiles of his time.
Lycortas of Megalopolis was a leading Achæan statesman and father of the historian Polybius. Philopœmen was the famous Achæan general.
The Messenians had put Philopœmen to death after capturing him in battle, which is why the Achæans banished them.
The Achæans had supported Rome against Philip of Macedon, the Ætolians and Antiochus the Great, king of Syria.

literary_notes.text: Rome sends mediators who bring the Achæans' sworn enemies with them, so the supposed peacemaking is plainly partisan.
The jeering and the one-sided vote show Appius as openly biased and contemptuous of Achæan dignity.
The long list of past services set against neglect and favoured exiles makes the Achæans' ingratitude-driven grievance feel bitter.
